title: Path traversal in pack-deploy endpoints allows reading files outside the industry-packs tree
description: The `packId` and `scopeDirName` parameters of the pack-deploy endpoints (`GET /api/packs/onboarding/:packId/:scopeDirName`, `POST /api/packs/deploy`) are used directly in filesystem path construction (`join(baseDir, 'industry-pack-' + packId)`, `join(packDir, 'scopes', scopeDirName)`) without any traversal or containment check. An authenticated user can supply traversal sequences (e.g. `a/../../` and `../`-chains) to make the service read files outside the `industry-packs` directory tree and return their contents.
impact: Read-only local file disclosure: an authenticated attacker can read the contents of any file with the fixed names consumed by the service (`onboarding.json`, `scope.json`, `sop.md`, `SKILL.md`, `initial-memories.json`, `workflow-plan.json`, `manifest.json`) located anywhere on the server filesystem reachable by the backend process. No write or execute primitive was demonstrated: the appended filenames are fixed, so arbitrary-name files (e.g. `.env`, `package.json`, SSH keys) cannot be read directly, and all writes go through mocked/DB paths that only copy already-read content.
technical_analysis: `getOnboardingConfig` in `src/services/pack-deploy.service.ts` builds paths as `join(baseDir, 'industry-pack-' + packId)` and `join(packDir, 'scopes', scopeDirName)` where `baseDir = resolve(process.cwd(), '..', 'industry-packs')`. Node's `join` does not reject `..` segments, and the prefix string `industry-pack-` is neutralized by supplying `packId = 'a/../../'` — the resulting segment `industry-pack-a` is canceled by the following `..`, so `packDir` resolves to the parent of the packs base directory, which exists and therefore passes the `existsSync` guard. `scopeDirName` then completes the escape to any directory, and `onboarding.json` inside it is read and returned. The same unvalidated pattern is used in `deploy()` (scope metadata, agents, skills, SOP, workflow reads). Fastify decodes URL-encoded parameters (`%2F`, `%2E%2E`) before they reach the handler, so encoded traversal survives route matching. Only the `authenticate` preHandler protects these routes — any authenticated user of any organization can call them, with no role or admin restriction.
poc_description:
1. Run the PoC test `npx vitest run tests/unit/pack-deploy-traversal.poc.test.ts` in `super-agent/backend` (test file added in this assessment).
2. The test starts a real Fastify instance registering the genuine `packDeployRoutes` with a mocked `authenticate` that accepts any Bearer token.
3. Create a marker file `onboarding.json` containing `TRAVERSAL-MARKER-9f31ab` in a temp directory outside `industry-packs/`.
4. Issue `GET /api/packs/onboarding/a%2F..%2F..%2F..%2F<relative-escape>%2Fleaked-scope` with any Bearer token: `packId = a/../../` resolves `packDir` above the packs base directory (the `industry-pack-a` segment is canceled by the following `..`), and `scopeDirName` traverses from there to the temp directory.
5. Observe HTTP 200 with the marker file's contents returned in `data`.
6. A control request with a nonexistent in-root pack returns `data: null`, and a request without a Bearer token returns 401.
remediation_steps: Validate that `packId` and `scopeDirName` match a strict allowlist pattern (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$`, no slashes or dots) before any path construction. Independently, after resolving the pack and scope directories, canonicalize with `resolve()` and verify the result starts with the canonical packs base directory plus path separator, rejecting otherwise. Apply the same check to the `deploy` flow, which shares the identical join pattern and additionally reads `scope.json`, agents, skills, SOP, and workflow files from the traversed directory.
evidence:
Vitest run against the real service and routes (mocked auth/DB only):

```text
✓ tests/unit/pack-deploy-traversal.poc.test.ts (4 tests) 118ms
  ✓ unauthenticated requests are rejected (authenticate preHandler is enforced)
  ✓ URL-encoded ../ traversal reads onboarding.json outside the industry-packs tree
  ✓ benign in-root control returns null for a nonexistent scope
  ✓ direct service-level call (bypassing routing) also traverses
```

The traversal test asserts `body.data.secret === 'TRAVERSAL-MARKER-9f31ab'`, a value written to a marker file in a temp directory outside `industry-packs/`, proving an out-of-root read.
assumptions: Requires any authenticated user of the backend (any role — `authenticate` is the only preHandler; no role or admin check). The backend's working directory must be the `backend/` folder so `getPacksBaseDir()` resolves to the sibling `industry-packs/` directory, which is the documented run layout.
counterevidence: The `authenticate` preHandler is enforced on every pack route (verified by the 401 control test), so this is not unauthenticated. The final file read always appends a fixed filename (`onboarding.json`, `scope.json`, `sop.md`, `SKILL.md`, `manifest.json`, `initial-memories.json`, `workflow-plan.json`), so the attacker cannot read arbitrary filenames such as `package.json`, `.env`, or SSH keys — only files with those fixed names outside the pack tree. JSON parse failures are caught and return null (onboarding path) rather than erroring. No WAF or path sanitization exists on this path (locally verified), but the filename constraint is a real ceiling on impact.
severity_change_conditions: Discovery of any code path where the fixed appended filename is attacker-influenced (e.g. an endpoint accepting a filename within a scope directory), or confirmation that sensitive files with the consumed fixed names exist in reachable directories, would raise the severity.

title: Cross-organization IDOR in knowledge-base routes (read/modify/delete of other orgs' KBs, files, folders)
description: Knowledge-base routes accept bare resource UUIDs and pass them to service methods that filter only by primary key, with no organization_id constraint. An authenticated member of any organization can read, rename, move, tag, or soft/hard-delete knowledge bases, folders, and files belonging to other organizations.
impact: Cross-tenant disclosure and destruction of another organization's knowledge-base content: file names, tags, sizes and metadata are returned by listFiles; display names/tags/folder assignments can be rewritten (updateFile, batchMoveFiles, batchAddTags); files can be hard-deleted (deleteFile, batchDeleteFiles); entire knowledge bases can be renamed or soft-deleted (update, delete). PoC: 9/9 assertions green.
technical_analysis: Every KnowledgeBaseService method that operates on an existing object filters only by primary key and never by organization_id: `findById` (where: {id}), `update` (where: {id}), `delete` (where: {id}), `listFiles` (where: {knowledge_base_id}), `updateFile`/`deleteFile` (where: {id}), `batchMoveFiles`/`batchDeleteFiles`/`batchAddTags` (where: {id: {in: fileIds}}), `listFolders`, `renameFolder`, `deleteFolder`, `getScopeBindings`, `updateStats`. The routes in knowledge-base.routes.ts pass request.params.id/fileId/folderId/scopeId straight into these methods with no ownership check. The only preHandlers are `authenticate` (identity only) and `requireModifyAccess`, which is `requireRole('owner','admin','member')` — a role check with no org binding, so any org's member qualifies. Only `listByOrganization` scopes by `request.user!.orgId`. Prisma's schema has organization_id on all these tables, so the fix is to include it in every where clause.
poc_description: Run `npx vitest run tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts` in super-agent/backend. The test mocks prisma with an in-memory store that filters records strictly by the where clause the production code passes, stubs only token verification to install an org-A member identity, then drives the real route handlers via fastify.inject against an org-B KB/file. All six C1 assertions pass: cross-org read (KB + file listing), update, file metadata rewrite, file deletion, KB rename, and KB soft-delete all succeed for the org-A member.
poc_script_code:
```bash
cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts
# → Test Files  1 passed | Tests  9 passed
# Evidence assertions (tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts):
#  - GET /api/knowledge-bases/{KB_B}          → 200, data.organization_id === ORG_B
#  - GET /api/knowledge-bases/{KB_B}/files    → items include 'SECRET-MARKER'
#  - PUT  /api/knowledge-bases/{KB_B}/files/{FILE_B} {display_name:'PWNED-BY-ORG-A'} → 200
#  - DELETE /api/knowledge-bases/{KB_B}/files/{FILE_B} → 204, store now empty
#  - PUT  /api/knowledge-bases/{KB_B} {name:'Renamed-by-OrgA'} → 200
#  - DELETE /api/knowledge-bases/{KB_B}        → 204, status='deleted'
```
remediation_steps: Add organization_id derived from request.user.orgId to every where clause on these paths: change findById/update/delete to filter by {id, organization_id} (findFirst), filter listFiles by organization_id alongside knowledge_base_id, filter updateFile/deleteFile/batchMoveFiles/batchDeleteFiles/batchAddTags/updateStats, and validate that knowledge_base_id-scoped routes (folders, bindings, tags) first load the KB scoped to the caller's org. The only org-scoped method today is listByOrganization.
evidence: PoC run (vitest, 9/9 passed): org A member issues GET /api/knowledge-bases/<KB_B> → 200 with organization_id=ORG_B, name='Org B private KB'; GET /api/knowledge-bases/<KB_B>/files → items containing display_name='SECRET-MARKER'; PUT /:id/files/:fileId with {display_name:'PWNED-BY-ORG-A'} → 200 and store mutated; DELETE /:id/files/:fileId → 204 and org B file removed; PUT /:id → KB renamed; DELETE /:id → KB status='deleted'; briefing PoC under separate report. No 403/404 was returned on any cross-org request; the only status codes were 200/204.
assumptions: Authenticated user of any role in any organization; knowledge of a target KB/file UUID (obtainable from logs, exports, notifications, or the org-scoped listing of one's own org's IDs after a cross-tenant leak).
counterevidence: Checked for guards that could neutralize this: (1) authenticate (src/middleware/auth.ts) only verifies identity — it does not bind the request to any resource; (2) requireModifyAccess is requireRole('owner','admin','member') — a plain member of ANY org passes, so it constrains nothing cross-org; (3) no requireScopeAccess preHandler or app-level hook guards these routes (verified src/app.ts registerRoutes wiring); (4) listByOrganization IS correctly org-scoped, so the listing endpoint does not leak foreign IDs directly — an attacker needs the target UUID from another source, and UUIDv4 enumeration is impractical; (5) kb upload route does check existence but not ownership, so upload to a foreign KB also succeeds if the UUID is known. These constraints reduce the attack's ease but do not restore tenant isolation.
confidence_rationale: Executed PoC through the real route handlers and real service functions with a where-clause-faithful in-memory prisma; 9/9 tests green. Only the transport (JWT verification) was stubbed, which is upstream of the broken control.
severity_change_conditions: Evidence that any UUIDs are exposed cross-org (e.g. in logs, exports, analytics, or the briefings/bindings endpoints) would confirm mass exploitability; conversely nothing observed lowers it.

title: Cross-organization access on briefing routes (read/mark-read/archive other orgs' briefings)
description: All four briefing endpoints under /api/business-scopes/:scopeId/briefings filter only by business_scope_id with no organization or scope-membership check. An authenticated user of any organization can read another org's briefing feed (titles, summaries, agent identities) and mutate its state (mark read, archive).
impact: Cross-tenant disclosure of another organization's briefing content (titles, summaries, categories, statuses, agent display names) plus unauthorized state changes (mark-read, archive) that suppress those briefings for the victim org's users.
technical_analysis: src/routes/briefing.routes.ts queries prisma.scope_briefings with where: {business_scope_id: scopeId, ...} for list/count/groupBy and where: {id, business_scope_id: scopeId} for the mark-read and archive updates. The scope_briefings and business_scopes tables both carry organization_id, but no query references it. The sole preHandler is authenticate, which populates request.user (id/orgId/role) and performs no authorization; unlike several other route files, no scopeAccess middleware is attached here. Therefore request.user.orgId is available but unused, and any org's scope UUID grants full read and state mutation of that scope's briefings.
poc_description: Run `npx vitest run tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts` in super-agent/backend — the C4 describe block drives the real briefing route handlers with an org-A member identity against an org-B scope and briefing, using an in-memory prisma whose filtering mirrors exactly the where clauses the production code builds.
poc_script_code:
```bash
cd super-agent/backend && npx vitest run tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts
# C4 assertions (all green):
#  GET    /api/business-scopes/{SCOPE_B}/briefings            → 200, contains 'SECRET-BRIEFING'
#  PATCH  /api/business-scopes/{SCOPE_B}/briefings/{id}/read   → 200, is_read=true
#  DELETE /api/business-scopes/{SCOPE_B}/briefings/{id}        → 200, is_archived=true
```
remediation_steps: Resolve the business scope first with an organization_id (or scope membership) constraint — e.g. load business_scopes by {id, organization_id: request.user.orgId} (or via scope_memberships) and 404 on miss — and add organization_id to every scope_briefings where clause, including the findMany, counts, groupBy, and the update filters.
evidence: PoC run in the same file as the KB IDOR (tests/unit/kb-idor.poc.test.ts, C4 describe block, 3/3 passed): GET /api/business-scopes/{SCOPE_B}/briefings returned HTTP 200 with a briefing titled 'SECRET-BRIEFING' (organization_id ORG_B) to an org-A member; PATCH .../read set is_read=true; DELETE set is_archived=true. No 403/404 on any cross-org request.
assumptions: Authenticated user of any org; knowledge of the target business-scope UUID (internal org data, logs, or client bundles; business_scopes uses UUIDv4 so blind enumeration is impractical).
counterevidence: Checked: (1) authenticate resolves identity but performs no scope-membership or org check; (2) no requireScopeAccess preHandler is attached to any briefing route (other route files use it, this one does not); (3) scope_briefings carries organization_id in the schema but the queries never reference it; (4) the PATCH/DELETE filters use {id, business_scope_id} — that binds to the scope but the scope itself is unauthenticated, so it adds no tenant protection; (5) UUIDv4 scope IDs make blind enumeration impractical. Severity reflects that briefings are agent-generated summaries (potentially business-sensitive) and the writes are limited to read/archive flags rather than content.
confidence_rationale: Same executed-PoC basis as vuln-0002: real route handlers and prisma where clauses against a faithful in-memory store; only token verification stubbed.
severity_change_conditions: Proof that briefing summaries contain credentials or highly sensitive business data would raise integrity/confidentiality impact; confirmation that scope UUIDs are broadly exposed (logs/exports) would confirm exploitability at scale.

title: Path traversal in workspace provisioning via unsanitized skill/agent names (workspace-manager.ts)
description: Skill and agent names are stored and later used in filesystem path joins (workspace-manager.ts) without any sanitization or containment check. An authenticated org user who creates a skill or agent with a `../`-containing name causes the backend, when provisioning a chat session workspace, to write files (SKILL.md, agent .md, or a copied skill directory) to attacker-chosen locations outside the intended `.claude/skills` and `.claude/agents` directories on the server.
impact: An authenticated org user can make the backend write arbitrary-content files (SKILL.md content / agent markdown with a controlled system prompt, or a full copied skill directory) to arbitrary relative paths reachable from the workspace base directory — e.g. overwriting application configs, other tenants' workspaces, cron/system files writable by the service user, or planting files that a later interpreter loads. File content includes substantial attacker-controlled text (skill body/description, agent systemPrompt). Demonstrated locally with synthetic markers reading the written files back outside the skills/agents roots.
technical_analysis:
Root cause is the absence of both input validation at creation time and containment checks at write time.

**Unvalidated creation path.** `POST /api/skills` (skills.routes.ts:50-54) accepts `{ name, display_name, ... }` with only a TypeScript interface — no zod/JSON-schema validation on `name`. `skillService.createSkill` (skill.service.ts:77-89) stores `input.name` verbatim to Postgres (`skills.name VARCHAR(255)`, no format constraint in prisma/schema.prisma:265). Similarly `createAgentSchema` (agent.schema.ts:17-21) enforces only min/max length and non-whitespace — `../../evil` passes. Notably, agent and skill names flow into `ScopeForWorkspace` (chat.service.ts) unmodified.

**Missing containment at the sink.** `WorkspaceManager.downloadSkill` (workspace-manager.ts:968-1044) computes `const skillDir = join(targetDir, skill.name)` with no containment check — unlike `readWorkspaceFile` (workspace-manager.ts:1474-1476), which explicitly rejects paths escaping `workspacePath`. The same unchecked join pattern exists in `generateAgentSubagentFiles` (workspace-manager.ts:756, `join(skillsDir, skill.name)` and :785 `${agent.name}.md`), `installSkillToWorkspace` (workspace-manager.ts:1359-1362, `join(skillsDir, skillName)` + `cp -r`), and `syncSkills` (workspace-manager.ts:862-883, removes/creates skill dirs by name). A `../` sequence in a name escapes the per-session workspace entirely: `join(skillsDir, '../../../../../../x')` resolves above the workspace base directory.

These sinks run during session provisioning (`ensureSessionWorkspace`, workspace-manager.ts:250-307), triggered whenever a chat session is created in a scope whose agents reference the crafted skill, and during workspace refresh on skill sync. Contrast: `createDocGroupSymlinks` (workspace-manager.ts:278) sanitizes document-group names with `replace(/[/\\:*?"<>|]/g, '-')` — the codebase sanitizes this same class of user data elsewhere but not for skills/agents.
poc_description: 1. Create a skill via POST /api/skills with name `../../../../../../escaped-skill` and a body/description (no route/service validation exists). 2. Attach the skill to a business scope/agent so it enters SkillForWorkspace. 3. Start a chat session; ensureSessionWorkspace calls downloadSkill which computes join(skillsDir, skill.name) and writes SKILL.md there. 4. Observe the marker file written outside the skills directory. Repeat with an agent named `../../../../../evil-agent` (generateAgentSubagentFiles writes `${agent.name}.md` into agentsDir) and with installSkillToWorkspace (skillName joined into skillsDir then cp -r).
remediation_steps: Enforce a strict name format at the API boundary: validate skill and agent names with a schema (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$`, no `/`, `\`, or leading dots) in the create/update routes and services, and reject existing stored names that violate it before workspace provisioning. Defense in depth: in WorkspaceManager, apply the same containment check used by `readWorkspaceFile` (resolve the joined path and verify it starts with the intended skills/agents directory) in `downloadSkill`, `generateAgentSubagentFiles`, `installSkillToWorkspace`, and when syncing/removing stale skill directories.
evidence: Vitest run (real WorkspaceManager from the repository, mocked S3 client, scratch base dir /tmp/trav-poc/workspaces): 3 tests passed. (1) downloadSkill with name `../../../../../../escaped-skill` and an inline body → log "[downloadSkill] Wrote inline skill \"../../../../../../escaped-skill\" from metadata body"; file `<base>/escaped-skill/SKILL.md` exists and contains the marker; control skill `normal-skill` correctly lands inside `.claude/skills/normal-skill/SKILL.md`. (2) generateAgentSubagentFiles with agent name `../../../../../evil-agent` → `<base>/org1/evil-agent.md` exists containing the marker prompt. (3) installSkillToWorkspace with skillName `../../../../../../copied-out` → `<base>/copied-out/SKILL.md` exists containing the marker. Contrast: readWorkspaceFile (workspace-manager.ts:1474-1476) rejects the same class of input via a prefix containment check.
assumptions: Requires an authenticated org user who can create a skill (POST /api/skills) or agent (POST /api/agents) with a crafted name, plus a chat session to be provisioned in that scope (or, for installSkillToWorkspace, a marketplace skill name containing traversal — route-layer control of that name was not audited end to end). Backend runs with filesystem write access to the workspace base directory and its ancestors.
counterevidence: Actively searched for controls: (1) skills.routes.ts has no JSON-schema or zod validation on POST / body name — only TypeScript interfaces; skill.service.ts createSkill passes input.name to the repository verbatim; updateSkill cannot change name but create can set any value. (2) The Prisma schema (skills.name VARCHAR(255)) and migration impose no format constraint — slashes and dots are valid characters. (3) The contrast control readWorkspaceFile at workspace-manager.ts:1474-1476 explicitly implements prefix containment, showing the codebase knows this pattern but did not apply it to skill/agent name joins. (4) Notably, document-group symlink names ARE sanitized with .replace(/[/\\:*?"<>|]/g, '-') (workspace-manager.ts:278), another proof sanitization exists elsewhere but not for skill/agent names. (5) Scope-generator-created skills and marketplace skills also feed these paths; I did not audit every name source, but the primary user-controlled route (POST /api/skills) is unvalidated, which alone establishes reachability. Searched for sanitization between service and workspace-manager (scope building in chat.service.ts/agent-runtime-claude.ts) — names are passed through as-is.
severity_change_conditions: Demonstrating that session workspaces are provisioned with the process owner able to write to a path that influences execution (e.g. another tenant's workspace, a service config, or a writable autoload directory) would raise confidentiality/availability and potentially the severity to high; if a name-format validation exists in an ingest layer not examined here (e.g. enterprise skill publish or import), reachability of the primary POST /api/skills route would need re-checking.

title: Missing authentication on avatar generation endpoints (POST /api/avatars/generate, /generate-batch)
description: POST /api/avatars/generate and POST /api/avatars/generate-batch lack the `authenticate` preHandler used by sibling avatar routes, so anonymous callers can invoke paid Nova Canvas image generation and write objects to the shared avatars S3 bucket when the feature flag is enabled.
impact: Unauthenticated resource consumption (AWS Bedrock Nova Canvas per-image cost) and unauthenticated writes to the global avatars/ S3 namespace. Data confidentiality is unaffected (generated keys are returned only to the caller); impact is cost abuse plus unauthenticated state change.
technical_analysis: In `src/routes/avatarRoutes.ts`, `POST /avatars/upload` registers `preHandler: [authenticate]`, but `POST /avatars/generate` (~line 50) and `POST /avatars/generate-batch` (~line 119) register only a JSON schema — no `preHandler`. `src/routes/index.ts` registers `avatarRoutes` with `prefix: '/api'` and no global authentication hook exists in `app.ts` (auth is per-route preHandler only), so these endpoints are reachable anonymously. The handlers call `avatarService.generateAvatar`, which invokes Bedrock Nova Canvas (`amazon.nova-canvas-v1:0`, a paid model) and uploads to S3 under a global `avatars/` namespace with no owner binding. A server-side `ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION === 'true'` gate exists, but it only controls the feature, not authentication.
poc_description: 1. Set ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION=true. 2. Send POST /api/avatars/generate with body {"role":"engineer"} and no Authorization header. 3. Observe 200 and an avatarKey — an S3 object written anonymously. 4. Repeat with POST /api/avatars/generate-batch with {"roles":[10 roles]} — all succeed anonymously.
remediation_steps: Add the `preHandler: [authenticate]` option to the POST /avatars/generate and POST /avatars/generate-batch route registrations in avatarRoutes.ts, matching the /avatars/upload route. Optionally add rate limiting and per-user quota for avatar generation.
evidence: Local vitest PoC (super-agent/backend/tests/unit/avatar-routes.authz.poc.test.ts, 6/6 passing) mounted the real avatarRoutes plugin with mocked auth/S3/Bedrock: anonymous POST /api/avatars/generate returned 200 with an avatarKey; anonymous POST /api/avatars/generate-batch returned 10/10 successful avatarKeys; no Authorization header sent on any request.
assumptions: Assumes ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION=true in the deployment; otherwise the endpoints return 400 (still unauthenticated, but no cost impact).
counterevidence: No auth middleware, ownership check, or rate limit exists on these routes — confirmed by mounting the real plugin. Mitigations found: ENABLE_AVATAR_GENERATION defaults to false (.env.example), batch is capped at 10 items, and generated keys are non-enumerable (Date.now + random suffix). These reduce but do not remove the issue when the feature is enabled.
confidence_rationale: Working local vitest PoC exercising the real route registration and real handler code with mocked S3/Bedrock; auth gap is visible in the route registration itself.
severity_change_conditions: If the flag is enabled by default in production deployments, severity rises to medium (confirmed cost abuse); a per-user rate limit plus auth would eliminate it.
